findings.headline: Business Rates income exceeded forecast by £294k
findings.detail: Gedling collected £6,185k in Business Rates against a budgeted estimate of £5,891k. This 5% favorable variance occurred in an uncertain rates environment and may indicate stronger business rate base growth, better collection performance, or timing effects.
findings.matters: Business Rates stability is critical to council sustainability, and material outperformance may indicate either forecasting conservatism or positive changes in the business tax base that strengthen future revenue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Outturn 2025-26 Variance Analysis
findings.headline: Capital programme experienced project deferrals at year-end, reducing planned capital spend
findings.detail: The Movement in Reserves analysis notes that capital financing requirements fell 'following project deferrals at outturn'. This means planned capital work was postponed or not delivered, requiring the council to reduce reserve drawdowns planned to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Capital deferrals, if cumulative, indicate the council may lack capacity to execute planned infrastructure renewal. This can signal either underfunding, project delivery risk, or resource constraints.
findings.figures: Not itemised in outturn; reference only to 'reduced capital programme financing'
findings.quote: Variance due to reduced capital programme financing following project deferrals at outturn

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Outturn 2025-26 Variance Analysis
findings.headline: Multiple licensing and fees income streams underperformed: taxi licensing £80k down, selective licensing £56k down
findings.detail: Taxi licensing income fell short by £80,213 ('lower than expected income'). Selective licensing income fell short by £56,463. Parks generated lower-than-expected income at car parks and the Solar Farm. Together these suggest either reduced demand for council services, or pricing that the market will not bear.
findings.matters: These are discretionary fee-earning services. Systematic underperformance across multiple revenue heads suggests either cyclical (post-COVID recovery) or structural (demand shift or pricing power loss) challenges. If structural, the council must rely more on central grant and council tax.
findings.figures: Taxi licensing shortfall £80,213; Selective licensing shortfall £56,463; Parks income shortfall £41,724
findings.quote: Variance due to lower than expected income

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Outturn 2025-26 Variance Analysis
findings.headline: Leisure center income has collapsed across multiple facilities, particularly Carlton Forum and Redhill
findings.detail: Carlton Forum Leisure Centre shows negative actual expenditure (−£4,941) on a £37,300 budget. Redhill Leisure Centre recorded actual spending of £144,362 against a budget of £266,300. The variance analysis attributes this to 'reduced income as fewer bookings which also leads to reduction in bar income'. The pattern affects multiple leisure centers, suggesting structural demand decline rather than one-off issues.
findings.matters: Leisure services are a discretionary revenue source that councils use to self-fund. Persistent booking shortfalls indicate either post-COVID recovery has stalled, or leisure demand has permanently shifted. This signals weaker revenue resilience and lower income to cross-subsidise other services.
findings.figures: Carlton Forum: budget £37,300, actual −£4,941; Redhill: budget £266,300, actual £144,362; Arnold Leisure: budget £480,800, actual £355,108
findings.quote: Variance mainly due to reduced income as fewer bookings which also leads to reduction in bar income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Outturn 2025-26 Variance Analysis
findings.headline: Corporate management spending nearly doubled: budget £601k, actual £1.07m, overspend £471k (78%)
findings.detail: This is the largest adverse variance in the council's accounts. The budget was £601,000 but actual spending reached £1,072,206. The variance is driven by 'additional salary related expenses' and notably, External Audit fees 'due to back dated invoices' — meaning the council is now paying audit invoices from prior periods that were not budgeted.
findings.matters: A 78% overspend on internal management costs raises questions about budget forecasting and financial control. Back-dated audit invoices suggest the council deferred payment of compliance costs in prior years, now falling due. For a lender, this indicates either weak controls or hidden liabilities.
findings.figures: Budget £601,000, Actual £1,072,206, Overspend £471,206
findings.quote: Variance due to increase banking charges, banking software charged along with External Audit fees due to back dated invoices

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Outturn 2025-26 Variance Analysis
findings.headline: Waste disposal costs surged 28% above budget, from £1.57m to £2.01m
findings.detail: Waste residual spending exceeded budget by £435,718 (actual £2,009,118 vs budget £1,573,400). The council attributes this to staffing cost allocation and undefined operational 'bin issues'. This is a statutory service the council cannot reduce or defer, making the overspend a material structural cost pressure.
findings.matters: Waste disposal is a non-discretionary service. A 28% budget miss suggests either cost inflation in disposal markets or volume growth the council failed to forecast. If this recurs, it will force cuts elsewhere or require reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Budget £1,573,400, Actual £2,009,118, Overspend £435,718
findings.quote: Variance due apportionment of staffing costs and bin issues offset by division R500 Waste Other

findings.headline: IT Replacement Reserve being spent down by £184,053
findings.detail: The IT Replacement Reserve is being drawn down in year-end variance by £184,053, from £822,923 opening to £638,871 closing. This shows the council is using this reserve to fund IT spending or refresh programmes.
findings.matters: Heavy drawdown of IT reserves may indicate necessary but unbudgeted IT spending, suggesting underlying asset management or infrastructure challenges.
findings.figures: Opening (822,923), year-end variance 184,053, closing (638,871)
findings.quote: IT Replacement Reserve (822,923) 184,053 (638,871)

findings.headline: NNDR Pool Reserve deteriorating further to £2.51m negative
findings.detail: The NNDR Pool Reserve, already negative at opening (£2.2m), has deteriorated further to (£2,507,650) in year-end, representing a worsening of approximately £308k. This is the largest single reserve and is moving in the wrong direction.
findings.matters: A deteriorating NNDR reserve indicates ongoing volatility or deficit in the non-domestic rates pool; this is a revenue risk that directly affects council cash flow and borrowing need.
findings.figures: Opening (2,199,935), year-end variance (2,507,650), deterioration ~£308k

findings.headline: Transformation Fund Reserve being drawn down heavily by £943,483
findings.detail: The Transformation Fund Reserve shows a major withdrawal of £943,483 in one of the budget scenarios, dropping from £1,323,647 opening to £380,164 in year-end. This indicates substantial transformation spending or unforeseen transformation costs.
findings.matters: Large transformation spend either signals the council is investing to improve efficiency, or that unplanned transformation costs are consuming reserves; either way, a lender wants visibility on why transformation reserves are being depleted rapidly.
findings.figures: Opening (1,323,647), withdrawal 943,483, closing (380,164)
findings.quote: Transformation Fund Reserve (1,323,647) 943,483 (380,164)

findings.headline: Total earmarked reserves declining from £8.59m to £7.92m over the year
findings.detail: The council's total earmarked reserves have reduced by £672,180 in the year-end variance. The opening balance of £8,593,594 closes at £7,921,414, indicating the council is drawing on reserves to manage its budget position.
findings.matters: Declining reserves are a key indicator of financial stress; a lender needs to know whether a council is eroding its financial buffer and how long reserves will sustain operations.
findings.figures: Opening balance (8,593,594), year-end variance (7,921,414), net reserve drawdown 672,180

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision expected July 2026 creates material uncertainty over future financial model and borrowing assumptions
findings.detail: Gedling remains uncertain about its future structure following LGR; the government decision on which unitary arrangement the council will join is expected in July 2026. Until confirmation, there is limited clarity on future operating model, service alignment, governance, and longer-term financial assumptions.
findings.matters: LGR creates fundamental uncertainty about the council's future size, revenue base, cost structure, and debt repayment capacity; a lender cannot reliably assess medium-term sustainability until the outcome is known.
findings.figures: Government decision expected July 2026
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation continues to create uncertainty for Gedling Borough Council in planning for the medium term, as the Council does not yet know which future unitary arrangement it will become part of. The Government's decision is expected in July 2026 and until that is confirmed, there remains limited clarity over the future operating model, service alignment, governance arrangements and longer-term financial assumptions.

findings.headline: Financing costs outturn at 4.62% significantly exceeds the approved indicator of 2.55%
findings.detail: The council's ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream came in at 4.62% against a budgeted 2.55%, representing an 81% variance. This metric measures the proportion of the revenue budget committed to debt service before any service delivery.
findings.matters: Higher-than-expected financing costs reduce the council's flexibility to fund services and respond to pressures; a lender needs confidence that debt service costs remain predictable and sustainable.
findings.figures: Actual ratio 4.62% vs approved indicator 2.55%
findings.quote: The outturn of 4.62% for service-related expenditure is higher than the approved indicator of 2.55% due to reduced Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) costs for 2025/26.

findings.headline: £1m property fund investment has declined to £893,935, losing 10.6% of value with a 6.32% entry fee already paid
findings.detail: The council holds a £1m investment in the CCLA Local Authority Property Fund made in 2017. The investment was valued at £936,770 on entry, immediately creating a 6.32% entry fee loss of £63,230. The current value at 31 March 2026 is £893,935, representing a total loss from the original £1m of £106,065 (10.6%). The investment declined by £59 during 2025/26 alone.
findings.matters: This is a material loss on a long-term investment; the combination of high entry fees and ongoing property market weakness suggests either a poor investment decision or exposure to market conditions affecting local authority finances.
findings.figures: Initial investment £1,000,000; entry fee £63,230 (6.32%); current value £893,935; total loss £106,065 (10.6%)
findings.quote: This valued the initial investment of £1m at £936,770, setting the implied entry fee at £63,230, or 6.32%. The certified value of the property fund investment at 31 March 2026 was £893,935 (down marginally from £893,994 at the end of March 2025) reflecting a loss in value of £59 during the 2025/26 year from.

findings.headline: Capital programme ran £965k below budget due to deferrals and slippage into future years
findings.detail: Capital expenditure outturn was £5.45m against an approved budget of £6.41m. This underspend reflects deferrals of schemes to 2026/27 and other programme variations during the year, resulting in a lower-than-planned Capital Financing Requirement (£18.4m vs £21.2m expected).
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage suggests delivery challenges; deferred spending moves borrowing needs to future years, affecting future budget headroom and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £5,448,183 vs approved £6,413,400; CFR outturn £18,443k vs original estimate £21,226k
findings.quote: The 2025/26 variance on the CFR is due to deferrals and savings on the 2025/26 capital programme, both of which reduced the borrowing requirement in that year, and to amendments on the capital programme during 2025/26, including the deferral of schemes to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council is relying on reserves to cover borrowing needs, with internal borrowing at 45% of capital requirement
findings.detail: Gedling is maintaining an 'internal borrowing' position where the Capital Financing Requirement (£18.4m) is not fully covered by external loans (£10.8m). Instead, cash in reserves is being used as a temporary measure. The internal borrowing ratio of 45% is slightly higher than the approved indicator of 41%, indicating growing reliance on reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing is only sustainable if reserves remain adequate; if reserves deplete, the council will need external borrowing at whatever rates apply then, potentially at cost.
findings.figures: CFR £18,443k vs total external debt £10,812k; internal borrowing 45% vs indicator 41%
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an "internal borrowing" position, ie. The underlying borrowing need (CFR) has not yet been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves and balances is being used as a temporary measure. The current projected outturn for internal borrowing is 45%, which is slightly higher than the approved indicator of 41%.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn and Budget Carry Forwards 202526
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates ongoing governance uncertainty, with government decision on Gedling's future unitary status not expected until July 2026.
findings.detail: Gedling remains uncertain about its post-reorganisation operating model, service alignment, and governance arrangements. The government decision on which unitary structure it will join was expected July 2026. This creates material uncertainty in medium-term financial planning.
findings.matters: Structural governance uncertainty affects medium-term financial planning, service viability, and the council's ability to execute strategic initiatives until the post-LGR arrangements are confirmed.
findings.figures: Government decision expected July 2026; timeframe of uncertainty ongoing at report publication (25 June 2026)
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation continues to create uncertainty for Gedling Borough Council in planning for the medium term, as the Council does not yet know which future unitary arrangement it will become part of. The Government's decision is expected in July 2026.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn and Budget Carry Forwards 202526
findings.headline: Capital programme carries forward 21% of budget (£1.5m) to 2026/27, indicating project delivery or planning challenges.
findings.detail: Gedling carried forward £1,517,500 of its £7,180,500 capital budget, representing significant re-profiling. Vehicle replacement delays accounted for £422,700 due to delivery lead times, with fire door replacement and other schemes also deferred to 2026/27.
findings.matters: High capital carry-forward levels suggest challenges in project execution or planning that may affect the council's ability to deliver its capital programme on schedule.
findings.figures: £1,517,500 carry forwards out of £7,180,500 budget (21%); vehicle replacement delays £422,700
findings.quote: The capital carry forward requests total £1,517,500 against the current approved capital programme of £7,180,500, representing 21% re-profiling for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn and Budget Carry Forwards 202526
findings.headline: Building Regulations trading account ran a deficit following years of losses, and the council has outsourced the service entirely.
findings.detail: The Building Regulations service recorded a £74,915 deficit in 2025/26 following a deficit position in prior years. After conducting a service review, the council transferred all building control services to the Erewash and West Nottinghamshire Building Consultancy effective 1 June 2026, indicating inability to sustain this statutory function within budget.
findings.matters: The council could not maintain financial viability of a statutory service and outsourced it, suggesting operational or cost control limitations.
findings.figures: £74,915 deficit in 2025/26; deficit position over multiple prior years
findings.quote: A service review was undertaken in 2025/26 following a deficit position over a number of years. From 1 June 2026, all building control services previously undertaken by Gedling Borough Council are being provided by the Erewash and West Nottinghamshire Building Consultancy.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn and Budget Carry Forwards 202526
findings.headline: Waste and Environmental Services overspent by £820,197 against original budget, with efficiency programme delivering only 44% of planned savings.
findings.detail: Environmental Services overspent by £820,197 compared to original budget due to continued reliance on agency staff during service transformation. The council's efficiency programme delivered only £308,000 of £703,200 planned, with £147,700 deferred and £247,000 removed as non-deliverable. Delays in waste management system implementation and restructure were the main causes.
findings.matters: Failed savings plans and escalating uncontrolled costs in a core service indicate financial management and operational transformation risks.
findings.figures: £820,197 overspend vs original budget; £333,681 overspend vs latest approved; efficiency delivered £308,000 of £703,200 planned (44%)
findings.quote: Environmental Services, including Waste, Street Care, and Transport and Fleet, this had a £333,681 controllable overspend at outturn against latest approved budget however this equates to an overspend of £820,197 when compared to the original budget.

findings.headline: Inflation and cost of living creating squeeze on both expenditure and income sources
findings.detail: Inflation remained above Bank of England's 2% target throughout 2025/26, affecting pay, utilities, fuel and contracted services costs. Simultaneously, cost of living pressures created uncertainty around council tax collection, business rates performance and fees and charges income while increasing demand for council services.
findings.matters: Costs rising (pay, energy, contracts) while income sources become uncertain; together threatens financial sustainability and requires active budget management.
findings.figures: Inflation above Bank of England's 2% target for much of the period; no specific rate stated
findings.quote: These factors, alongside continuing cost of living pressures, increased demand for some services and support to vulnerable households, while also creating uncertainty around fees and charges income, council tax collection, business rate performance and local economic growth.

findings.headline: Ongoing workforce capacity constraints including vacancies, skills gaps and interim staffing reliance
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies persistent workforce capacity issues including vacancies, specialist skills shortages, service demand pressures and reliance on interim arrangements, with expectation these will continue through Local Government Reorganisation period.
findings.matters: Capacity constraints restrict service delivery and control implementation; reliance on interim staffing increases costs; affects financial resilience and governance compliance.
findings.figures: Not quantified; described as ongoing issues without specific resolution timeline
findings.quote: Work remains ongoing to mitigate workforce capacity issues, including vacancies, specialist skills shortages, service demand pressures and reliance on interim arrangements, particularly in the run-up to Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: People Services received only limited assurance rating amid governance transition
findings.detail: People Services was the only audit function to receive limited assurance rating in 2025/26. The council attributes this to transition and change of governance structure, identifying it as a 'known area of concern', and states action has been taken to improve controls.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates control gaps or weaknesses in a key function affecting workforce management and payroll; suggests increased risk during organisational transition.
findings.figures: 1 limited assurance audit in portfolio vs. substantial assurance or above for other areas
findings.quote: the People Services review which was the only limited assurance audit this year. Although, due to the Council's transition and change of governance structure, this was a known area of concern and action has been taken to improve controls in this area.

findings.headline: Unrecovered fraud loss of £606,593 remains outstanding and under insurance claim negotiation
findings.detail: A sophisticated fraud discovered in July 2022 totalled £934,343. The council recovered £327,750 from the Nottinghamshire Local Government Pension Scheme in 2022/23, but the remaining £606,593 is being pursued via an insurance claim which is currently under negotiation with the insurance company.
findings.matters: Represents material funds not available to the council; recovery is uncertain and dependent on insurance settlement completion.
findings.figures: £934,343 total loss; £327,750 recovered; £606,593 outstanding
findings.quote: The financial impact of the fraudulent activity has been quantified as £934,343. During 2022/23, £327,750 was recovered from the Nottinghamshire Local Government Pension Scheme, leaving a balance of £606,593 which is currently being pursued through an insurance claim.

findings.headline: Council pursuing multi-year audit recovery via reduced-scope Proof-in-Total method rather than full audit, starting 2025/26.
findings.detail: Rather than a full audit, Gedling will undertake a Proof-in-Total audit in 2025/26 focused on balance sheet reconstruction and reserve classification. Progression to full audit in 2026/27 depends on demonstrating robust financial reporting capacity, timely working papers, and no material issues in 2025/26, subject to auditor risk assessment and central technical team approval.
findings.matters: Full audit assurance will not be restored until at least 2026/27. A lender needs to understand that normal audit oversight is suspended during this recovery period, and any failures in interim-year reporting could delay return to full scope further.
findings.quote: If no material issues arise, move to a full audit with Proof in Total in 2026/27, subject to approval by our central technical team.

findings.headline: Auditors cannot confirm whether historic ledger transactions have been deleted or modified following IT control weaknesses exposed by a 2021/22 fraud conviction.
findings.detail: A member of Gedling's finance team was convicted of fraud in 2021/22, which exposed IT control weaknesses in the financial ledger. Four years later, auditors have been unable to obtain sufficient evidence from the council's IT team and ledger provider to confirm the completeness and integrity of historic ledger transactions. The unresolved issue means the council cannot receive full audit sign-off; auditors indicate they hope to focus on this during 2025/26.
findings.matters: For a lender, financial statements are only trustworthy if the underlying ledger can be verified as complete and unaltered. A compromise of ledger integrity due to fraud-exposed control weaknesses means the council's stated financial position cannot be independently validated.
findings.figures: 2021/22 (fraud conviction); 2025/26 (planned focus for resolution)
findings.quote: The fraud exposed IT control weaknesses over the financial ledger, adding complexity to the Council's position. This increased audit risk as we needed to obtain assurance that the historic ledger transactions were complete.

findings.paper_title: 14a Appendix 1 Corporate risk register report Q4 2025 26
findings.headline: Agresso financial system control risks accepted as unaffordable to remediate
findings.detail: The council's SLT has determined that some fraud risk within the Agresso financial system must be accepted because mitigation options are undeliverable within reasonable cost. User access is now centralised in ICR, which has reduced fraud risk, but residual risk remains deliberately unmitigated.
findings.matters: Accepted internal control weaknesses in the core financial system mean fraud risks are not fully mitigated; this is a material governance and audit concern for lenders assessing control environment
findings.figures: Agresso user access centralisation completed; some mitigation options deemed unaffordable
findings.quote: The Agresso system risk is currently being considered by SLT who have determined that some risk will need to be accepted due to some option being undeliverable within a reasonable cost.

findings.paper_title: 14a Appendix 1 Corporate risk register report Q4 2025 26
findings.headline: Staff notices in finance and property services likely to impact capacity in next quarter
findings.detail: The council notes that notice from staff in finance and property services is likely to have an impact in the next reporting period. This follows capacity assessment for local government reorganisation and existing capacity challenges across the council.
findings.matters: Loss of finance staff directly affects the council's financial management capability at a time when it is managing significant budget pressures and LGR transition
findings.figures: Finance and Property services staff notices flagged for Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: Capacity continues to be something to watch but no rise in risk levels in Q4, notice from some staff in finance and Property services is likely to impact next reporting period.

findings.paper_title: 14a Appendix 1 Corporate risk register report Q4 2025 26
findings.headline: Planned 2026/27 budget efficiencies undeliverable due to LGR, requiring replacement or MTFP adjustment
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget was approved as balanced with new efficiencies identified, but transformation work originally planned will not proceed due to local government reorganisation. The longer-term efficiencies this was expected to deliver will not materialise and must either be replaced with new efficiencies or removed from the medium-term financial plan.
findings.matters: A material element of the approved budget plan is now undeliverable, creating near-term pressure on the MTFP that requires active resolution before it cascades to future years
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget approved as balanced in March; transformation efficiencies now undeliverable
findings.quote: New efficiencies were identified and approved, however but has become apparent that due to some transformation work now not being undertaken in light of LGR the longer erm efficiencies will not be realised and will need to come out of the MTFP or be replaced by new efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: 14a Appendix 1 Corporate risk register report Q4 2025 26
findings.headline: Current year significant overspends from staffing issues, offset by savings but with continuing risk
findings.detail: The council has experienced material overspends linked to staffing and related service issues in the environment department. These have been managed through offsetting savings elsewhere, but the register confirms the risk of continuing overspends remains significant until the underlying service and staffing issues are resolved. Dedicated finance resource has been deployed for analytical work, but this is not expected to conclude quickly.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends indicate structural budget management problems that remain unresolved, creating ongoing pressure on the council's financial position
findings.figures: Environment department staffing-driven overspends requiring ongoing management
findings.quote: Some overspends relating to staffing issues and related service issues have resulted in significant overspends. Whilst these have been offset by savings generated in other areas the risk of continuing overspends remains significant until service and staffing issues can be resolved.

findings.headline: The council is introducing a new rolling capital programme for temporary accommodation maintenance, funded by borrowing, signalling ongoing housing pressure.
findings.detail: A new £50,000 annual capital scheme has been added to fund maintenance of temporary accommodation housing stock. This is a new recurring commitment funded from prudential borrowing, indicating sustained pressure on homelessness or temporary housing that the council expects to persist across the medium term.
findings.matters: Growing temporary accommodation provision is a marker of housing market stress and rising demand on council resources. A lender tracking a council's balance sheet needs to know whether this demand is temporary or structural, and whether it will absorb budget pressure in the coming years.
findings.figures: £50,000 annual rolling programme 2026/27–2030/31; funded by prudential borrowing
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation stock maintenance programme £50,000. A provision to ensure temporary accommodation housing stock is maintained, addressing any issues identified by the condition surveys. This is to be funded through prudential borrowing.

findings.headline: The council expects a large capital receipt of £10.8m but has earmarked most of it contingent on Carlton Active passing a deferred business case.
findings.detail: The council is planning to receive approximately £10,837,400 in capital receipts from asset disposals. However, the document states the remainder (after funding the initial capital programme) 'will be earmarked for the Leisure Transformation - Carlton Active project pending a financially viable business case'. This means most of the receipt is held back pending a decision not yet made, reducing the council's liquidity and flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender depends on understanding where the council's cash is and whether it is truly available. Tying up most of a large receipt to a contingent project—with no certainty on timing or outcome—reduces borrowing headroom and increases execution risk.
findings.figures: £10,837,400 expected capital receipt; £6,911,000 of it earmarked for Carlton Active pending business case
findings.quote: The Council is expected to receive a large capital receipt of around £10,837,400, some of which will be used to fund the proposed Capital Programme, however the remainder will be earmarked for the Leisure Transformation - Carlton Active project pending a financially viable business case.

findings.headline: The council is drawing down £1.37m from its NNDR Pool reserve in a single year to fund the Carlton Active design stage, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The largest single source of direct revenue financing for 2026/27 capital is a £1,370,000 transfer from the NNDR Pool reserve to fund Carlton Active design and demolition costs. This is a material depletion of a strategic reserve in one year, leaving less buffer for future pressures or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion in the context of LGR uncertainty and unproven leisure centre economics suggests the council is committing financial resources to a contingent project with limited flexibility to reverse course or absorb losses.
findings.figures: £1,370,000 from NNDR Pool reserve in 2026/27; total direct revenue financing for capital £1,423,000
findings.quote: £1,370,000 contribution from the NNDR Pool reserve to fund the RIBA 3 & 4 and demolition costs for Carlton Active project.

findings.headline: Carlton Active leisure centre project commits £2.12m to design and demolition, but the full business case is not yet proven and abortive cost risk exists.
findings.detail: The council is moving from concept design (RIBA 2) to detailed design (RIBA 3 & 4) and demolition for a new leisure centre at Carlton. High-level financial modelling suggests it is viable with 50% council funding and 50% borrowing, but the council explicitly states 'a full Business case will be undertaken as part of this next stage once costs certainty is known' to ensure 'income generation is sufficient to cover the required costs of borrowing'. Should the scheme not proceed, pre-construction costs incurred to date become abortive.
findings.matters: A lender bears the risk if the centre's projected income does not materialise and the council cannot service the debt, or if cost overruns force additional borrowing. The fact the business case is deferred to the next design stage signals the current financial model is incomplete.
findings.figures: £2,120,000 for RIBA 3 & 4 and demolition; funding mix 50% council resources, 50% borrowing
findings.quote: Should the scheme not go ahead the pre-construction costs incurred to date will be abortive costs. A full Business case will be undertaken as part of this next stage once costs certainty is known to ensure that the project is financially viable and the income generation is sufficient to cover the required costs of borrowing.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will force the council to rewrite capital plans from April 2028, making all post-vesting-day forecasts provisional.
findings.detail: The council has vesting day expected on 1 April 2028 when a new unitary authority takes over. The council says this 'will have an impact on any capital investments post vesting day' and signals it may need to 'approve a new capital programme to align with the dissolution of Gedling Borough Council'. For now it is presenting five-year plans but acknowledges these may not hold.
findings.matters: A structural reorganisation this close (18 months away) means capital commitments made now may be void, services may transfer, and borrowing terms could shift. A lender needs to know whether debt commitments survive the reorganisation and who is liable.
findings.figures: Vesting day 1 April 2028; £10,194,000 capital programme 2026/27; indicative £5,189,700 for 2029/30 and £4,944,200 for 2030/31
findings.quote: Gedling Borough Council is preparing for Local Government Reorganisation, with Vesting Day expected on 1 April 2028. The creation of a new Unitary Council which Gedling is expected to be a part of will have an impact on any capital investments post vesting day, however for the purpose of the 2026/27 budget Gedling will continue to present a full three-year capital programme with an indicative programme for 2029/30 and 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Prudential and Treasury Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Statement (TMSS) 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure plan drops 54% between first and second year (£10.2m to £4.7m)
findings.detail: The council's capital programme shows service investment of £10,194k in 2026/27, falling sharply to £4,696k in 2027/28 (54% reduction) and remaining at £4,562k in 2028/29. The document states this has been 'fully factored into the Council's Medium Term Financial Plan', but the cliff between year 1 and year 2 is striking and suggests either major projects completing or capital plans constrained by budget pressure.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether this drop is planned and driven by project completion, or is being forced by financial constraint. Combined with the stated 'significant budgetary pressures', it suggests capital priorities are being deferred.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure: 2026/27 Estimate £000s 10,194.0  2027/28 Estimate £000s 4,696.0  2028/29 Estimate £000s 4,562.0

findings.paper_title: Prudential and Treasury Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Statement (TMSS) 2026/27
findings.headline: £1m property fund investment down 4.5%, and accounting override protecting it from revenue loss expires in 2029
findings.detail: The council's investment in the CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund has declined from £0.937m (December 2017) to £0.895m (31 December 2025), a loss of £42k. Unrealised capital losses are currently deferred from the revenue account under a statutory IFRS9 override that expires 31 March 2029. After that date, all movements in the fund's value will immediately hit the General Fund. An earmarked reserve has been set aside to mitigate risk, but its size is not disclosed.
findings.matters: This creates a revenue volatility risk from 2029 onwards unless the override is extended. If the property market falls and the override lapses, a further decline in this £1m investment will immediately damage the General Fund. The reserve mitigation is opaque.
findings.figures: Investment value 31 Dec 2025: £0.895m (loss of £0.042m from original £0.937m in Dec 2017). Annual dividend: circa £38k.
findings.quote: The initial value of the Council's £1m investment in the CCLA Property Fund in December 2017 was £0.937m. The latest value as at 31 December 2025 is £0.895m... An earmarked reserve has been set aside to mitigate the risk to the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Prudential and Treasury Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Statement (TMSS) 2026/27
findings.headline: Council explicitly cites significant budgetary pressures and declines voluntary MRP contribution
findings.detail: The council states it will make no voluntary revenue provision (VRP) above the statutory minimum for MRP in 2026/27, citing both economic climate and 'significant budgetary pressures'. This continues a pattern—the council has made no voluntary MRP contributions in previous years either. Voluntary MRP is a discretionary buffer councils deploy when finances allow; declining it signals financial constraint.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would read this as direct confirmation the council is under budget strain and managing to cash rather than deploying reserves to accelerate debt repayment.
findings.figures: Statutory MRP charge for 2026/27: £1,346,872. No voluntary contribution. Net revenue stream 2026/27: £16,882.3k.
findings.quote: In view of the economic climate and significant budgetary pressures, the Council will not provide for an additional voluntary contribution to MRP in 2026/27, and neither has it done so in previous years.

findings.headline: Demand for capital resources substantially exceeds available funding
findings.detail: The Council states that 'Demand for capital resources to meet investment needs and aspirations will exceed the resources available to the Council.' Projects below 15 points are disregarded unless they are statutory or health & safety issues, forcing prioritisation by rigid scoring criteria.
findings.matters: Unmet capital needs indicate either deferred maintenance creating future cost pressures or continued service constraints affecting council operations and borrowing risk.
findings.figures: Total capital programme 2026/27: £10,194,000; of which £3,903,700 must be borrowed
findings.quote: Demand for capital resources to meet investment needs and aspirations will exceed the resources available to the Council and so are prioritised as follows:

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for April 2028 creates significant planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The Council has introduced a 'Gedling Legacy Plan 2026-2028 which will remain in place until Local Government Reorganisation takes place in April 2028.' This signals the Council will cease to exist in its current form in 16 months, creating uncertainty around capital project delivery and financial continuity.
findings.matters: Reorganisation in April 2028 creates material uncertainty for multi-year capital projects and the Council's future financial position, affecting both project delivery and loan repayment prospects.
findings.figures: Local Government Reorganisation April 2028; Strategy covers period to 2030/31
findings.quote: The Cabinet agenda sees the introduction of a Gedling Legacy Plan 2026-2028 which will remain in place until Local Government Reorganisation takes place in April 2028.

findings.headline: Capital grant funding is diminishing as government cuts to Local Government continue
findings.detail: The document notes that 'capital grants are now diminishing in number as further cuts are enforced on Local Government.' New Homes Bonus, previously a capital funding source, is 'not expected to be a source of capital funding going forward.'
findings.matters: Declining grant funding forces the Council to either reduce capital ambitions or increase borrowing, both of which have negative revenue consequences.
findings.figures: Grants and contributions in capital programme: £4,159,800 in 2026/27; £3,336,000 in 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Unfortunately capital grants are now diminishing in number as further cuts are enforced on Local Government.

findings.headline: The Council is not asset-rich and capital receipts are becoming severely limited
findings.detail: The Council explicitly states it is 'not asset rich' and that 'the ability to realise significant capital receipts is becoming limited.' This constrains one of the main sources of capital financing and suggests limited flexibility to fund projects outside grant-dependent schemes.
findings.matters: Limited capital receipts force reliance on borrowing or external grants, reducing financial flexibility and increasing debt service costs from an already-tight revenue budget.
findings.figures: Capital receipts budgeted at £707,500 in 2026/27, declining to £125,000 in subsequent years
findings.quote: However, the Council is not asset rich and the ability to realise significant capital receipts is becoming limited.

findings.headline: A £3.9m borrowing requirement in 2026/27 on a revenue budget operating at very tight margins
findings.detail: The capital programme requires £3,903,700 in prudential borrowing for 2026/27, with the Council explicitly warning that borrowing 'will be tightly controlled due to the financial impact it will have on a revenue budget that already operates to very tight margins.' This signals constrained revenue capacity to service debt.
findings.matters: Significant borrowing on an already-tight revenue budget increases financial risk and reduces the council's capacity to absorb service pressures or unexpected costs.
findings.quote: Prudential borrowing will be tightly controlled due to the financial impact it will have on a revenue budget that already operates to very tight margins.

findings.headline: High and rising dependency on discretionary fee income and Council Tax as grant funding shrinks
findings.detail: Real-terms grant funding is falling (cash grants reduced by £0.012m in 2026/27 and expected to fall further). The Council is planning to increase discretionary income by 3.5% annually (£130,100 in 2026/27) and has assumed 2.99% Council Tax increases every year through 2030/31. However, the cost-of-living crisis is flagged as a risk to discretionary service income: 'The cost-of-living crisis presents an additional risk to income levels for discretionary services.' The paper notes restrictions on surplus-generating fees mean 'income not being able to be used to fund other core services.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's revenue assumptions are achievable. Rising reliance on discretionary fees and maxed-out Council Tax (already at or near referendum limits) leaves no flexibility. Recession or further cost-of-living deterioration directly threatens both income streams.
findings.figures: 3.5% discretionary income inflation in 2026/27 (£130,100); 2.99% Council Tax increases assumed for all five years; Council Tax increase of £5.82 per Band D in 2026/27 approaches the 3% or £5 referendum trigger
findings.quote: The Council will increasingly rely on income generated by local fees and charges, and council tax, and these will need to be consistently increased year on year to offset the momentum of continual reductions in available budgets. However, restrictions placed on surplus generating fees results in income not being able to be used to fund other core services. The cost-of-living crisis presents an additional risk to income levels for discretionary services

findings.headline: Pay awards and inflationary pressures creating sustained budget headwinds with limited mitigation
findings.detail: The Council is absorbing a 3% pay award for 2026/27 (£563,400 cost, partially offset by prior-year underspend of £150,000). The paper explicitly flags 'This level of pay claim presents a downside risk to the current MTFP projections' and notes concerns about 'market adjustments that may be required to address skill shortages in key service areas.' The MTFP assumes only 2% pay awards from 2029/30 onwards, which may be optimistic given current public sector labour market conditions.
findings.matters: Pay costs are structural and unavoidable. If actual awards exceed the 2% assumption in the outer years of the MTFP, or if the council must make market adjustments to retain staff during the merger transition, the already-thin reserves will be pressured further.
findings.figures: 3% pay award 2026/27 costs £563,400; 2% assumed from 2029/30 onwards; no contingency stated for higher awards or market adjustments
findings.quote: Salary increases of 3% and the increase in employers' national insurance contributions continue to have a significant impact on the Councils budget across the medium-term... This level of pay claim presents a downside risk to the current MTFP projections

findings.headline: Previous year's £374,000 of efficiency savings removed as undeliverable, raising questions about delivery capability
findings.detail: The Council's efficiency programme had previously agreed to £4.47m of reductions. During 2025/26, £374,000 of these were formally removed as 'deemed undeliverable' and replaced with new proposals totalling £449,300. This suggests a gap between planned and achievable savings. A risk provision of £142,200 is included in the current budget specifically 'to manage the inherent risks of efficiency programme delivery.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that savings plans will land. When councils retrospectively remove large tranches of agreed savings and add contingency provisions, it signals execution risk and potential future budget pressures.
findings.figures: £374,000 removed as undeliverable in 2025/26; replaced by £449,300 in new proposals; £142,200 risk provision for delivery failures
findings.quote: Subsequently a report was approved by Cabinet to remove £374,000 of approved efficiencies from the total programme as they were deemed undeliverable

findings.headline: Food waste collections mandate underfunded by approximately £1m annually with uncertain grant support
findings.detail: A statutory regulatory requirement to introduce food waste collections is adding circa £1m of annual cost to the council. The Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant covers this in 2026/27 (£1.3m budgeted), but DEFRA has only confirmed funding for one year. The council acknowledges that loss of the EPR grant 'would cause a significant challenge to balance its budgets requiring an additional £2m of efficiencies to be delivered by the end of 2028/29.'
findings.matters: This is a mandated cost with uncertain funding. If EPR is withdrawn, the council faces either service cuts or further reserve drawdowns, neither of which improves financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £250,000 pilot allocation; £1,304,800 EPR funding in 2026/27; £1,203,700 in 2027/28; council states regulatory change cost is 'circa £1m' and unfunded
findings.quote: significant pressures including the introduction of food waste collections (circa £1m) have not been adequately funded in the settlement, meaning the Council will have to rely on the use of the general fund reserve to fund these pressures and balance the budget

findings.headline: Structural deficit means the council will exhaust its reserves by 2029, forcing service cuts
findings.detail: The General Fund Balance will decline from £5.67m (2026/27) to £1.30m by 2030/31, reaching its minimum required level by 2029/30. From that point, the council forecasts no further capacity to address funding gaps. The paper states the 'structural deficit that remains in the Medium Term Financial Plan is now significant' and expects service delivery contraction if efficiency plans do not proceed as expected.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can maintain service provision and debt servicing capacity over the medium term. When reserves reach minimum levels with no buffer, the council becomes vulnerable to any adverse variance.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance declining from £5,669,600 (2026/27) to £1,300,600 (2030/31); minimum required balance of £1,266,200 means from 2029/30 the council will have no discretionary reserves
findings.quote: From 31 March 2029 onwards the budget forecasts the General Fund will be operating at minimum levels with no further capacity to address funding gaps, indicating the increasing risk presented to the Council's financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: 4a. Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report 24-25 - Gedling
findings.headline: Gedling is one of 24 councils facing ongoing legal action initiated by Thurrock Council over APSE membership.
findings.detail: Thurrock Council has initiated legal proceedings against 23 other local authorities that are members of the Association for Public Service Excellence (APSE), including Gedling. The auditors identified this as a significant matter requiring management discussion during the audit. No detail is provided in the report about the nature of the claim or potential financial exposure.
findings.matters: Unresolved legal action against the council represents potential financial liability and reputational risk. The involvement of 24 councils suggests a sector-wide dispute of potential scale. The council's exposure and likely costs should be assessed.
findings.figures: 23 other councils involved (24 total including Gedling)
findings.quote: Implications of the ongoing legal action initiated by Thurrock Council against 23 other local authorities, including Gedling Borough Council, that are members of the Association for Public Service Excellence (APSE).

findings.paper_title: 4a. Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report 24-25 - Gedling
findings.headline: Former council officer found guilty of fraud valued at nearly £1m in October 2024, exposing significant IT control deficiencies.
findings.detail: An officer dismissed in 2022 was convicted of fraud by abuse of position valued at nearly £1m. An Internal Audit review (April 2023 to January 2024) found significant deficiencies in controls including privileged user access and payment controls. The council has subsequently reduced privileged system access from 15 to 3 users, though remediation is still ongoing.
findings.matters: A £1m fraud loss combined with identified control weaknesses in IT systems and payment processing represent material governance and operational risk. The three-year lag between fraud discovery and conviction suggests weaknesses in investigative controls. Current remediation efforts do not fully restore confidence given the scale of historic loss.
findings.figures: nearly £1m; privileged access reduced from 15 to 3 users
findings.quote: In October 2024, a former Council Officer, who was dismissed in 2022, was found guilty of fraud by abuse of position, to the value of nearly £1m.

findings.paper_title: 4a. Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report 24-25 - Gedling
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on financial statements for third consecutive year.
findings.detail: The auditor cannot express an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements due to insufficient time to rebuild assurance following prior-year disclaimers for 2022, 2023, and 2024. The disclaimer will be issued by the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. Three consecutive years without audit opinion means no independent verification of the council's reported financial position.
findings.matters: No audit assurance on financial statements for three consecutive years is a fundamental concern for lenders evaluating creditworthiness and for finance directors managing council resources. It prevents verification of opening balances and raises questions about the reliability of reported financial positions.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion. For this reason, we will be issuing a disclaimed opinion in time for the Council to publish its financial statements by the backstop date of 27 February 2026 as required by the relevant legislation.

news_drafts.lead: Using reserves less than planned suggests either improved spending discipline or that planned expenditure did not materialise, both of which indicate better-than-expected financial management.

news_drafts.lead: A council building reserves when budgeted to draw them down signals better control of spending or stronger-than-expected income, indicating improved financial resilience and reduced pressure on borrowing.

news_drafts.headline: Business Rates income exceeded forecast by £294k
news_drafts.lead: Business Rates stability is critical to council sustainability, and material outperformance may indicate either forecasting conservatism or positive changes in the business tax base that strengthen future revenue.
